paper.title: Survivors' Mental Health and the Protective Role of Income Stability
paper.code_data_availability: No replication-package or openICPSR statement appears in the main text. …

registers.role: sample frame; demographics; family linkages identifying partners (married or cohabiting) and children

registers.years: 1985–2018 (the paper states that death dates are included from 1970 onward)
registers.role: treatment: date of the spouse's death, used to restrict to fatal index events

registers.name_in_paper: National Patient Registry – Administrative Records (Landspatientregisteret – Administrative Oplysninger, LPR-ADM)
registers.years: 1977–2018 (the paper states records are consistently measured from 1980 through 2018)
registers.role: treatment / sample frame: admission dates and location of all visits to public or private hospitals, used to identify the index heart attack or stroke hospitalization

registers.name_in_paper: National Patient Registry – Diagnoses (Landspatientregisteret – Diagnoser, LPR-DIAG)
registers.role: treatment: ICD diagnoses used to identify heart attacks and strokes
variables_mentioned: diagnoses using the International Classification of Diseases system

registers.years: 1985–2018 (the paper states the register is available from 1980)
registers.role: treatment moderator and controls: annual flows of all sources of income, including earnings, government transfers from all programs (DI, sick pay, early retirement, OAP, unemployment insurance), payouts from retirement savings accounts, payouts from insurance companies and capital income; used to build household income, the household income loss and the instrument

registers.years: 1977–2018 (the paper states prescription data are used from 1995 onward)
registers.role: outcome: prescription pickup dates and ATC codes of all prescription drugs purchased from pharmacies in Denmark; psycholeptics (N05) and psychoanaleptics (N06) define the mental health outcome
controls: educational attainment (seven education categories in the additional set of controls)
controls: visits to psychiatrists, used for heterogeneity analysis by mental health at baseline and for the indicator for prior psychiatric treatment
controls: visits to psychiatrists from 1990 onward

linkages: Family linkages in the Population Registry (BEF) identify partners (married or cohabiting) and children; couples are defined by marriage or cohabitation as of five years prior to the health event

Hospital admissions and diagnoses (LPR-ADM, LPR-DIAG) are linked at the individual level to death records (DOD) to identify fatal heart attack and stroke events (death within 12 months of the index admission)
Prescription records (LMDB) are linked to the consumer; the paper notes that more than 99 percent of these drugs can be linked directly to the consumer
Income (IND) is summed across both spouses to form household income; pension annuities received by the surviving spouse show up in the survivor's tax records

sample.universe: The entire Danish population from 1995 through 2018, with administrative individual-level data and family linkages; the universe of Danish households
sample.unit_of_observation: Household (surviving spouse) by event-time period — calendar year for the annual analysis and calendar month for the monthly analysis
selection_rules: One spouse is hospitalized for the first time in the hospitalization data with a heart attack or a stroke (the index event)
Restrict to fatal events: the spouse dies within 12 months of the index admission
Couples defined by marriage or cohabitation as of five years prior to the health event, to freely allow for changes in marital status
Both spouses are Danish residents and aged 45–80 in the year of the index event
Exclude self-employed individuals, because the data only contain wages and net profits
Balance the sample from four years before to four years after the index event (so the surviving spouse does not die within this window)
Treatment group: spouse's fatal event in year τ; control group: spouse's fatal event in year τ + Δ with Δ = 5, assigned a placebo event in τ
sample.period: Data 1995–2018. Main analysis (Figure 1): treatment-group fatal events in 1999–2013, control-group events in 2004–2018 with a placebo event assigned five years earlier. Figure 2: health events 1999–2015 with death within three years. Figure 3: health events 1999–2013 with death within 12 months.
sample.n_observations: 21,182 households in the pooled Table 1 estimation (7,129 with a male and 14,053 with a female surviving spouse); Table 1 is estimated on observations for years −1 and 0

construction_notes: Event time r is normalized to the assigned event year: r = year − τ, with r = 0 the year of the assigned event; the monthly analysis uses the same normalization around the month of the health event

Mental health outcome: indicator for redeeming at least one prescription for a psycholeptic (ATC N05) or psychoanaleptic (ATC N06) drug; extensive margin only; annual take-up is defined as redeeming a prescription at least once within a given year, and the annual effects therefore capture cumulative effects over months within a year

Household income loss: the change in household income from the last full year before the shock (r = −1) to the first full year after the shock (r = 1), normalized by baseline income in r = −1, i.e. the percent change in household income from the year before to the year after the event
In Figure 3 and Table 1 the household income loss is winsorized at its top and bottom 1 percent; in Table 1 it is also normalized at the mean of individuals in the treatment group

Instrument: the share of overall household income earned by the deceased spouse in the baseline year (r = −1), entered jointly as an indicator for earner / nonearner and a second-order polynomial in the share
The main components of household income are labor earnings (33 percent), payments from DI and OAP (31 percent), and payments from retirement plans (18 percent)
Mean household income loss is 0.304 overall, 0.286 among male and 0.313 among female surviving spouses (standard deviations 0.144, 0.142 and 0.143); medians 0.299, 0.276 and 0.308
Seventy-four percent (79 percent) of deceased spouses did not have earnings at baseline among households with female (male) survivors
Annual out-of-pocket spending on psycholeptics and psychoanaleptics averages DKK 389 (US $60) among those who consume any of these drugs in the year of the spousal death
Δ = 5 in the main analysis (control households experience their fatal event five years after the treatment households); the post-event window is always smaller than Δ

Figure 3 Panel C reweights households where the deceased spouse was a nonearner using population weights from the gender-specific age distribution of households where the deceased spouse was an earner

claims.statement: Spousal death raises the take-up of mental health medication among all households (pooled over the gender of the surviving spouse) by 0.105 at month 0 relative to the baseline period (event month −1).

treatment.label: Spousal death (fatal heart attack or stroke of the spouse)

register_source.value: National Patient Registry (LPR-ADM, LPR-DIAG) for the index heart attack/stroke hospitalization and Death Registry (DOD) for the death date; couples identified via the Population Registry (BEF)

definition.value: Indicator for the surviving spouse's household belonging to the treatment group, i.e. the spouse was hospitalized for the first time with a heart attack or stroke (the index event) and died within 12 months of that admission; the control group consists of households whose spouse experiences the same type of fatal event Δ = 5 years later and is assigned a placebo event.

timing.value: Index hospitalization in event year 0; death within the following 12 months. Event time r is measured relative to the assigned event year (r = year − τ).

outcome.label: Take-up of mental health medication by the surviving spouse

register_source.value: Pharmaceutical Database (LMDB, Laegemiddeldatabasen): redeemed-prescription pickup dates and ATC codes N05, N06

definition.value: Indicator for whether the surviving spouse redeemed at least one prescription for a psycholeptic (ATC N05) or psychoanaleptic (ATC N06) drug in the period. Measured at both monthly and annual frequency; annual take-up is defined as redeeming a prescription at least once within a given year. The paper refers to responses in this variable as the impacts on "mental health".

timing.value: Monthly: calendar month r relative to the month of the index health event.

units.value: share of surviving spouses redeeming at least one N05/N06 prescription in the period (0–1 indicator), so 0.105 = 10.5 percentage points

magnitude.interpretation: corresponding to a 100 percent increase relative to the counterfactual in that month (10.4 percentage points = 20.9 percentage points − 10.5 percentage points)

estimand.target_population: Surviving spouses whose partner was hospitalized with a first heart attack or stroke and died within 12 months (the treatment group), aged 45–80 at baseline
estimand.time_horizon: month 0 relative to the health event (the first month of the event)

population.description: Surviving spouses in Danish households in which one spouse was hospitalized for a first heart attack or stroke and died within 12 months; couples married or cohabiting as of five years before the event, both spouses Danish residents aged 45–80 in the year of the index event, self-employed excluded, panel balanced from four years before to four years after the event.
population.ages: 45–80 in the year of the index event
population.period: Data 1995–2018; treatment-group fatal events in 1999–2013 and control-group fatal events in 2004–2018 (assigned a placebo event five years earlier)
subgroups_defined: Gender of the surviving spouse (males / females)
Degree of household income loss imposed by the shock
Earner status of the deceased spouse at baseline (earner / nonearner)
Presence of children younger than 18 / older than 18
Baseline household income level
population.selection: Conditioned on the couple experiencing a fatal spousal heart attack or stroke at some point in the sample period; both spouses Danish residents aged 45–80 at the index event; married or cohabiting as of five years before the event; self-employed excluded; the balanced panel requirement implies the surviving spouse did not die within the four years after the event.

identification.source_of_variation: The calendar timing of a spouse's fatal heart attack or stroke: households whose spouse has the fatal event in year τ (treatment) are compared with households whose spouse has the same type of fatal event in year τ + Δ, Δ = 5 (control), to whom a placebo event is assigned in year τ.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common (parallel) trends: absent the spousal death, the mental health outcomes of the treatment and control groups would have followed the same trend in the postperiod.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Visual inspection of the four pre-event years in raw data and a formal test that δ_r = 0 for all r < 0 from equation (1) with controls; the paper reports parallel pre-trends hold across all specifications and sample splits (Figure 1).

key_assumptions.assumption: Within a time window of Δ the specific year of spousal death is as good as random, so the timing of the death event is unrelated to unobserved determinants of the survivor's mental health.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the conjecture underlying the common-trends assumption; supported by closely parallel pre-trends and by the choice of Δ = 5, with Supplemental Appendix Table B.3 varying Δ from 3 to 7.

key_assumptions.assumption: The post-event window in the event studies is always smaller than Δ, so treatment and control groups are never both treated at the same point of the analysis horizon.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Design choice stated in Section II.A; Δ = 5 with effects identified up to four years after the spousal death.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the analysis conditions on couples who experience a fatal spousal health event in the sample period, on both spouses being Danish residents aged 45–80, on five years of prior marriage/cohabitation, on not being self-employed, and on a balanced panel (the surviving spouse does not die within the window).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Selection rules stated in the Analysis Sample subsection; Supplemental Appendix Table B.2 replicates the analysis on an unbalanced sample including surviving spouses present for any number of periods, with similar results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement: the take-up of mental health medication proxies the survivor's mental health; the paper notes observed responses also reflect the diagnostic process, the survivor's decision to seek care, and possible provider effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Caveat stated in the Variable Definitions subsection; universal, heavily subsidized health care means effects are not confounded by access to or affordability of care.

threats_discussed: Differential pre-event trends between treatment and control households
Challenges from units switching in and out of experimental arms, as posed by de Chaisemartin and d'Haultfoeuille (2024)
The same household can appear in both the treatment and the control group, which the paper addresses by clustering standard errors at the household level
Observed take-up of medication also reflects the diagnostic process, the survivor's decision to seek care, and possible provider effects
The choice of Δ trades off household similarity against the length of the analysis horizon
robustness_checks: Supplemental Appendix Figure B.3: restricting the sample to cases in which the cause of death matches the heart attack/stroke event (results unchanged)
Supplemental Appendix Table B.2: unbalanced sample including surviving spouses present for any number of periods (results similar)
Supplemental Appendix Table B.3: varying Δ from 3 to 7, and nonoverlapping treatment and control households (similar findings); Supplemental Appendix Figure B.8 visualizes this exercise
Formal test that δ_r = 0 for all r < 0 (pre-trends) from equation (1) with controls
unresolved_confounders: Observed take-up of mental health medication also reflects the diagnostic process, the survivor's decision to seek care, and possible provider effects (physician practice styles), which the paper flags as a caveat rather than resolving.

estimator.value: Dynamic difference-in-differences (OLS event study with household fixed effects), equation (1)

estimation.specification: Equation (1): y_{i,r} regressed on event-time indicators I_r, their interactions with Treat_i (coefficients δ_r), household fixed effects and controls X_{i,r}; r = −1 omitted. Estimated separately for male and female surviving spouses and at monthly and annual frequency.
controls: quadratic in the surviving spouse's age
year fixed effects (absorbing time trends in medication consumption)
indicators for time relative to the index health event
estimation.clustering: Standard errors clustered at the household level

sample_n.value: Balanced panel of treatment and control households, four years before to four years after the index event; the paper does not print N for Figure 1

source_table.value: Figure 1, Panel A, right-hand plot (monthly frequency), event month 0

adjustment_set.label: Quadratic in the surviving spouse's age
Indicators for time relative to the index health event (I_r)

heterogeneity.finding: Both the immediate and longer-run patterns are qualitatively similar across gender, with baseline levels and treatment effects that are somewhat larger among female surviving spouses.

ambiguities: Figure 1 plots 95 percent confidence intervals but prints no standard errors, interval endpoints or p-values, so statistical significance is recorded only where the paper asserts the effect in words.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.how: No standard error, confidence-interval endpoint or p-value is printed for δ_r. Figure 1 plots 95 percent confidence intervals graphically only, and the paper reports no numerical uncertainty for the dynamic estimates in the text or in a table.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.how: No standard error, confidence-interval endpoint or p-value is printed for δ_r. Figure 1 plots 95 percent confidence intervals graphically only, and the paper reports no numerical uncertainty for the dynamic estimates in the text or in a table.

The printed data labels in the right-hand panel were matched to their markers by horizontal position: the annual (black) series is labelled at event years 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 in increasing x-order and the monthly (purple) series is labelled once, at month 0. evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.how: No standard error, confidence-interval endpoint or p-value is printed for δ_r. Figure 1 plots 95 percent confidence intervals graphically only, and the paper reports no numerical uncertainty for the dynamic estimates in the text or in a table.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common (parallel) trends: absent the spousal death, the mental health outcomes of the treatment and control groups would have followed the same trend in the postperiod.

key_assumptions.assumption: Within a time window of Δ the specific year of spousal death is as good as random, so the timing of the death event is unrelated to unobserved determinants of the survivor's mental health.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as the conjecture underlying the common-trends assumption; supported by closely parallel pre-trends and by the choice of Δ = 5, with Supplemental Appendix Table B.3 varying Δ from 3 to 7.

key_assumptions.assumption: The post-event window in the event studies is always smaller than Δ, so treatment and control groups are never both treated at the same point of the analysis horizon.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.how: No standard error, confidence-interval endpoint or p-value is printed for δ_r. Figure 1 plots 95 percent confidence intervals graphically only, and the paper reports no numerical uncertainty for the dynamic estimates in the text or in a table.

The printed data labels in the right-hand panel were matched to their markers by horizontal position: the annual (black) series is labelled at event years 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 in increasing x-order and the monthly (purple) series is labelled once, at month 0. The labels whose values the text states explicitly (0.176 for year 0, 0.029 for year 4 and 0.105 for month 0 in Panel A; 0.158 and 0.184 for year 0 in Panels B and C) anchor the mapping, and 0.034 is the label at event year 4 of the annual series.

mediators_claimed: The income loss imposed by the spousal death: the paper's abstract states that a large share of the spike in take-up of mental health medication upon spousal death can be explained by this income loss, and reads the pattern as a liquidity rather than a permanent income effect.

heterogeneity.finding: The sensitivity of the event-year mental health effect to household income loss is somewhat stronger among female survivors (column 5) than among male survivors (column 3); footnote 9 states that the difference in the point estimates across males and females is statistically insignificant.

The paper reads the short-lived, event-year-only nature of the differentials by the deceased spouse's earner status (Figure 3, Panel C) as consistent with liquidity effects rather than permanent income effects.

ambiguities: Table 1 reports no significance stars, p-values or confidence intervals; statistical significance is recorded from the paper's own wording together with the t-ratio implied by the printed coefficient and standard error.

The specification is 2SLS, but the paper describes the heterogeneity analysis as correlational in nature; the estimand is recorded as a CATE (how the treatment effect varies with income loss) rather than as a causal effect of income on mental health.

evidence.annotation: The graphs present the F-statistic from a regression of the household's income loss on the share of household income earned by the deceased spouse (an indicator for positive earnings and a quadratic in the share), controlling for children indicators (presence of younger/adult children based on the age 18 cutoff) and the household's log income in the year before the event. Printed on the panel: "Males (F-statistic: 61.54)" and "Females (F-statistic: 101.54)".

evidence.how: Table 1 prints coefficients and standard errors only: no significance stars, p-values or confidence intervals are reported, and the table note reports the mean, median and standard deviation of household income loss but no mean or standard deviation of the outcome.

Implied t-ratio |0.7509| / 0.1304 = 5.76, computed from the printed coefficient and standard error, used together with the paper's own wording to record statistical significance; Table 1 prints no stars or p-values.

The paper's magnitude statement is the coefficient times the printed standard deviation of household income loss: 0.7509 x 0.144 = 0.1081, i.e. a 1 standard deviation change in income loss moves the event-year treatment effect by about 10.8 percentage points.

value.claimed_domain: Income-security / safety-net policy more broadly: the authors claim the welfare gains from income security programs can come in the form of improved mental health, and note that the Danish programs and policies they describe are broadly similar to those in other developed countries.
boundary_conditions: Denmark has no explicit survivors' benefit scheme, in contrast to US Disability Insurance
Health care is universal, tax-funded and free at the point of use, and prescription drugs are heavily subsidized

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

mediators_claimed: The income loss imposed by the spousal death: the paper's abstract states that a large share of the spike in take-up of mental health medication upon spousal death can be explained by this income loss, and reads the pattern as a liquidity rather than a permanent income effect.

heterogeneity.finding: The sensitivity of the event-year mental health effect to household income loss is somewhat stronger among female survivors (column 5) than among male survivors (column 3); footnote 9 states that the difference in the point estimates across males and females is statistically insignificant.

The paper reads the short-lived, event-year-only nature of the differentials by the deceased spouse's earner status (Figure 3, Panel C) as consistent with liquidity effects rather than permanent income effects.

ambiguities: Table 1 reports no significance stars, p-values or confidence intervals; statistical significance is recorded from the paper's own wording together with the t-ratio implied by the printed coefficient and standard error.

The specification is 2SLS, but the paper describes the heterogeneity analysis as correlational in nature; the estimand is recorded as a CATE (how the treatment effect varies with income loss) rather than as a causal effect of income on mental health.

Implied t-ratio |0.7519| / 0.1827 = 4.12, computed from the printed coefficient and standard error, used together with the paper's own wording to record statistical significance; Table 1 prints no stars or p-values.

The paper's magnitude statement is the coefficient times the printed standard deviation of household income loss: 0.7519 x 0.143 = 0.1075, i.e. a 1 standard deviation change in income loss moves the event-year treatment effect by about 10.8 percentage points.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common (parallel) trends: absent the spousal death, the mental health outcomes of the treatment and control groups would have followed the same trend in the postperiod.

key_assumptions.assumption: Within a time window of Δ the specific year of spousal death is as good as random, so the timing of the death event is unrelated to unobserved determinants of the survivor's mental health.

key_assumptions.assumption: The post-event window in the event studies is always smaller than Δ, so treatment and control groups are never both treated at the same point of the analysis horizon.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Design choice stated in Section II.A; Δ = 5 with effects identified up to four years after the spousal death.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the analysis conditions on couples who experience a fatal spousal health event in the sample period, on both spouses being Danish residents aged 45–80, on five years of prior marriage/cohabitation, on not being self-employed, and on a balanced panel (the surviving spouse does not die within the window).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Selection rules stated in the Analysis Sample subsection; Supplemental Appendix Table B.2 replicates the analysis on an unbalanced sample including surviving spouses present for any number of periods, with similar results.

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement: the take-up of mental health medication proxies the survivor's mental health; the paper notes observed responses also reflect the diagnostic process, the survivor's decision to seek care, and possible provider effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Caveat stated in the Variable Definitions subsection; universal, heavily subsidized health care means effects are not confounded by access to or affordability of care.

heterogeneity.finding: The paper reports that parallel pre-trends tightly hold across all specifications and sample splits, including the pooled sample and the male and female panels of Figure 1.

ambiguities: The paper reports the pre-trend test only verbally and visually; no pre-period coefficient, standard error or p-value is printed, so the point estimate and uncertainty are recorded as absent and significance is recorded as false on the strength of the paper's own statement.

The paper states that the test is run for all r < 0 and that pre-trends hold across all specifications and sample splits, so this single claim stands for the pooled and both gender panels rather than one coefficient in one panel.

evidence.annotation: Notes: This figure studies the take-up of mental health medication around a spousal death by the gender of the surviving spouse. The treatment group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a fatal heart attack or stroke in 1999 – 2013, and the control group consists of individuals whose spouse experiences a similar event but in 2004 – 2018 (to whom we assign a placebo event five years earlier), where we restrict the sample such that both spouses are in the age range of 45 – 80 at baseline. The sample is balanced across the four years before and after the health event so that each household appears throughout the analysis horizon. ... The panels on the right present the treatment effect of spousal death from the dynamic difference-in-differences specification in equation (1) estimated at a monthly frequency in purple along with estimates for annual frequency in black. The figures plot the estimates of δr along with their 95 percent confidence intervals, where the regressions include household fixed effects, time fixed effects, and a quadratic in the surviving spouse's age. The average take-up rate in month − 1 and year − 1 are, respectively, 0.104 and 0.251 among all households, 0.068 and 0.180 among male surviving spouses, and 0.120 and 0.284 among female surviving spouses.

evidence.how: The paper reports the result of the pre-trend test only in words and visually: no pre-period coefficient, standard error, joint test statistic or p-value is printed for the δ_r with r < 0, in the text, in Figure 1 or in a table.
